structure.overview: The case concerns the Applicant's challenge to a visa officer's decision refusing to extend and restore his study permit in Canada due to non-compliance with study permit conditions. The Applicant, who had academic interruptions and delayed permit renewal, sought judicial review of the refusal decision made by the immigration officer (tribunal_below). The Federal Court dismissed the application, finding the officer's decision reasonable and procedurally fair.

party_points.text: Applicant failed to meet study permit conditions and did not provide required documents
Decision is unreasonable and Respondent improperly supplemented Officer’s reasons
Inordinate delay in processing breached procedural fairness

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant requests the Court to set aside the Decision and have it redetermined by a different officer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court dismisses the Applicant's application for the reasons that follow.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant arrived in Canada in 2016 to study computer science at York University with a valid study permit expiring November 19, 2019, requiring continuous study and departure upon expiry.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant renewed his Nigerian passport and had his temporary resident status restored and work-study permit extended to December 31, 2022, with conditions to continue studies at Lassonde and leave Canada by then.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: In 2021, the Applicant was barred from studies at Lassonde for two years due to poor academic performance, eligible for readmission in summer 2023.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: On June 27, 2022, the Applicant was accepted into a one-year music program at Humber College.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: On October 26, 2022, the Applicant applied to extend his study permit under subsection 182(1) of the IRPR.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227
citations.why: Cites the regulation under which the extension was applied.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On January 17, 2023, a visa officer refused the Applicant's extension due to insufficient funds; the study permit expired December 31, 2022, and the Applicant did not challenge this.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: On February 22, 2023, the Applicant applied to IRCC to restore and extend his expired study permit.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: On April 27, 2023, the Applicant was notified that additional information was required to support his application.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: On May 2, 2023, the Applicant’s lawyer submitted additional documents stating the Applicant completed his program and sought extension to qualify for a post-graduate work permit.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant applied for leave to challenge the Decision on July 4, 2023; the Court granted leave on June 19, 2024.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Study permit decisions are reviewed on a reasonableness standard, as established in Vavilov at paragraphs 10 and 23.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65
citations.why: States the reasonableness standard for review of study permit decisions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasonableness review requires decisions to be transparent, intelligible, justified, and based on a rational chain of analysis per Vavilov.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Judicial review requires finding a central or significant error to render the decision unreasonable, per Vavilov.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65
citations.why: Sets threshold for judicial review intervention.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Procedural fairness issues are reviewed on correctness or akin to correctness, considering fairness standards in context.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65
citations.why: States standard for procedural fairness review.

citations.cite: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69
citations.why: Supports correctness standard for procedural fairness.

citations.cite: Chera v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 733
citations.why: Explains fairness standards to be applied.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Public information states students must not take leave exceeding 150 days or they must change status or leave Canada, else they breach study permit conditions.

citations.cite: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, “Study Permits: Assessing study permit conditions” (last modified 25 September 2023), online: <canada.ca>
citations.why: Provides official guidance on study permit conditions and leave limits.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent argues the Applicant failed to meet study permit conditions and did not provide required documents, making the Decision reasonable.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant contends the Decision is unreasonable and that the Respondent improperly supplemented the Officer’s reasons in their memorandum.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court disagrees that the Respondent supplemented the Officer’s reasons; the memorandum aligns with the Officer’s notes and reasons.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Respondent’s memorandum summary is consistent with the Officer’s reasons, referencing the Applicant’s non-compliance with study permit conditions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer’s reasons are clear, intelligible, and reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court cites Ntamag confirming that restoration is not allowed if the student is not enrolled or actively pursuing studies under subsection 220.1(1).

citations.cite: Ntamag v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FC 40
citations.why: Confirms restoration disallowed if not enrolled or actively studying.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant was barred from studies in 2021 and did not resume studies until September 2022, thus not enrolled or actively studying for over a year.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Although the Applicant started a new program in September 2022, he lacked prior authorization and delayed renewing his study permit until near expiration.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer’s finding that the Applicant failed to comply with study permit conditions by not being actively engaged in study is reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant’s sole purpose to restore his permit for PGWP eligibility justifies the Officer’s conclusion that restoration requirements were unmet, per Ofori.

citations.cite: Ofori v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 212
citations.why: Supports refusal when restoration sought solely for PGWP eligibility.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant’s persistent non-compliance renders him ineligible for restoration despite timely application within 90 days.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer reasonably considered the Applicant’s history and intention but found non-compliance with section 182 conditions, justifying refusal.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer noted the Applicant did not provide an updated Letter of Acceptance; the lawyer’s letter showed program completion and transcript submission.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer reasonably required an updated Letter of Acceptance since the Applicant had completed studies and sought extension only for PGWP eligibility.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with the Respondent that the issue of the Officer's decision on restoration is determinative of the judicial review application.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Breaches of procedural fairness are reviewed on a correctness standard focusing on fairness of process considering all circumstances.

citations.why: States correctness standard for procedural fairness breaches

citations.cite: Eagle’s Nest Youth Ranch Inc v Corman Park (Rural Municipality #344), 2016 SKCA 20 at para 20
citations.why: Supports correctness standard for procedural fairness

citations.cite: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43
citations.why: Confirms focus on fairness of process in procedural fairness review

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Procedural fairness is relaxed for study permit applications due to non-judicial nature and officers' expertise, per Li v Canada.

citations.cite: Li v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 791 at paras 45–50
citations.why: Supports relaxed procedural fairness in study permit context

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applicants must provide sufficient evidence; officers have no duty to allow addressing concerns from insufficient evidence, per Hassani and Huang.

citations.cite: Hassani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1283 at para 24
citations.why: Supports no duty on officers to allow addressing insufficient evidence

citations.cite: Huang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 145 at para 7

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argued that an 'inordinate delay' in processing breached procedural fairness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects the Applicant's delay argument, noting IRCC processing times are non-prescriptive and delays alone do not breach procedural fairness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant failed to provide all requested information timely despite IRCC's request and counsel's partial submission; no further steps were taken.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: IRCC's decision took time but delay was not inordinate, unfair, or prejudicial to the Applicant.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer reasonably denied restoration and extension due to Applicant's failure to comply with original permit conditions under IRPR subsections 182 and 220.

citations.why: Legal basis for denial of restoration and extension

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No questions for certification were posed or found by the court.
